item.research_question: How can the room temperature ductility of an initially brittle refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) with a continuous ordered B2 matrix be improved while maintaining high yield strength?
item.processing_route: 1. Vacuum/argon arc melting followed by hot isostatic pressing (HIP) at 1200 °C for 2 hours under 210 MPa argon. 2. Homogenization at 1200 °C for 24 hours followed by slow cooling (10 °C/min) to room temperature (Condition 1). 3. Solutionizing Condition 1 at 1400 °C for 20 min followed by water quenching (Condition 2). 4. Annealing Condition 2 at 600 °C for 120 hrs followed by water quenching (Condition 3).
item.test_conditions: Room temperature (RT) and 600 °C uniaxial compression testing at a strain rate of 0.001 s−1; Vickers microhardness (4.9 N load, 15 s dwell); Microstructural characterization via SEM, TEM, and Atom Probe Tomography (APT).
key_findings: Condition (1) (continuous B2 matrix) exhibited a yield strength of 2035 MPa but only 4.5% compressive strain before fracture.
Condition (2) (single-phase weakly ordered BCC) showed high ductility with no fracture after 60% true strain but lower yield strength (1065 MPa).
Condition (3) (inverted microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates in continuous BCC matrix) achieved a yield strength of 1345 MPa and 16.9% peak strain with fracture at 38% strain.
At 600 °C, Condition (3) showed anomalous strengthening with a yield strength of 1423 MPa (higher than its RT value of 1345 MPa) and 16.2% plasticity.
APT analysis revealed strong elemental partitioning: B2 phase is rich in Al and Zr, while BCC phase is rich in Nb and Ta.
The microstructure of Condition (3) consists of discrete B2 precipitates (~50 nm) within a continuous disordered BCC matrix, contrasting with Condition (1) where B2 is the continuous matrix.
Condition (1) hardness was 562 ± 16 HV, Condition (2) was 405 ± 11 HV, and Condition (3) was 475 ± 12 HV.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that the poor ductility in Condition (1) is caused by the continuous ordered B2 matrix, which is inherently brittle. The improved ductility in Condition (3) is attributed to the 'inversion' of the microstructure, where the continuous phase becomes the more ductile disordered BCC matrix, while the hard B2 phase exists as discrete precipitates providing strengthening. The anomalous strengthening at 600 °C in Condition (3) is speculated to result from competing slip systems in the complex B2 phase (e.g., <001>{110} and <111>{112}) leading to sessile kinks or dislocation debris, similar to mechanisms in Ni3Al.
item.limitations: The authors state that the details of the strengthening mechanisms are beyond the scope of the study and that the explanation for the anomalous strengthening at 600 °C is highly speculative. They note that applying classical precipitation hardening models requires parameters (lattice misfit, elastic properties, fault energies) that are difficult to quantify in this complex RHEA.
item.future_work: The authors recommend additional scientific studies to establish the influence of concentrated alloy additions on precipitation strengthening parameters, further investigation of deformation mechanisms at room temperature and 600 °C, and additional studies at higher temperatures and under tensile loading.
